title: One More Year
theme: God gives us time, but are we allowing Christ to make something of it?
opening: We often wonder why some lives end unexpectedly while others continue. But perhaps the more important question is not how much time we have been given, but what we are allowing God to do with it.
prayer: Lord Jesus,  Thank You for the life and time You have given me, and for the mercy that allows me to begin again.  Forgive me for the times I have kept You at a distance, whether through fear, pride, distraction, or feelings of unworthiness.  Help me recognize that You are not simply waiting for me to become fruitful, but offering Your love and guidance to help me grow.  Holy Spirit, soften what has become hardened within my heart. Give me the courage to welcome Your correction as well as Your comfort.  May the gifts You have placed within me grow into something that nourishes others and strengthens the Body of Christ.  And when my time on earth is complete, may I have lived not merely in Your presence, but in a relationship that allowed Your love to bear fruit through me.  Amen.
body:
In today's Gospel, Jesus speaks of two tragedies in which people lost their lives. He asks whether those who died were greater sinners than those who survived.

His answer is unmistakable: “By no means!”

Their deaths were not punishment for greater wrongdoing. Yet Jesus uses these tragedies to remind us that life is uncertain and repentance cannot always be postponed.

We do not know the time or hour of our death. But while we are alive, we have the opportunity to prepare our souls, examine our choices, and respond to God's grace.

Jesus then tells the parable of a fig tree planted in an orchard. For three years, the landowner has come looking for fruit, finding none. Finally, he tells the gardener to cut it down.

But the gardener asks for another year. He offers to cultivate the soil, nourish the tree, and give it another opportunity to bear fruit.

I find the three years interesting, considering that Jesus' public ministry is traditionally understood to have lasted approximately three years. Although the Gospel does not explicitly connect these periods, the parallel invites reflection.

During His ministry, Jesus taught, healed, forgave, and reached out to those who had been rejected or forgotten. He offered people the opportunity to change, yet not everyone recognized or accepted what He was offering.

I see ourselves in that fig tree, God the Father in the landowner, and Jesus in the gardener.

What moves me most is that the gardener does not simply ask for more time. He offers to do the work necessary for the tree to flourish.

How often do we overlook this in our relationship with Christ?

We may believe in Him, pray to Him, and acknowledge His presence, yet never fully understand how deeply He desires to participate in our lives.

Sometimes we feel unworthy of being close to Him. We imagine ourselves standing outside His circle, forgetting how far His love extends. Other times, we simply go about our lives without allowing Him to reach the places within us that need His attention.

And perhaps that is why the image of cultivation matters.

To nourish a tree, the gardener must work the soil around its roots. What has become hardened must be loosened. What is depleted must be replenished.

Could it be that we sometimes resist the very work Christ is trying to accomplish within us?

We welcome His comfort, but perhaps not always His correction. We desire His peace, yet hold tightly to the fears, judgments, and attachments that prevent us from receiving it.

The tree is alive, but it bears no fruit.

And I wonder whether we, too, can spend years believing in Christ without allowing that relationship to transform how we live.

Today's first reading from Ephesians brings another dimension to this understanding. Paul reminds us that Christ has given each of us gifts so that we may grow together in faith, no longer swept away by misleading teachings, but living the truth in love.

We are all part of the Body of Christ, and each of us has something to contribute.

A tree does not bear fruit for itself alone. Its fruit becomes nourishment for others.

Perhaps the same is true of the grace we receive. The patience, forgiveness, compassion, wisdom, and love that develop within us are meant to reach beyond ourselves.

And when we refuse to grow, something we might have offered to another remains unrealized.

The parable ends without telling us whether the fig tree eventually bears fruit.

That silence is meaningful.

The landowner has granted more time. The gardener has offered his labor. But the outcome remains unknown.

We may spend our lives asking God for more time, more answers, or more blessings, without recognizing that Christ is asking us to let Him work with what we have already been given.

Perhaps the greater tragedy is not that our lives will one day end, but that we might reach that day having never fully welcomed the relationship Christ was offering us.

We are still here. The gardener is still at work.

But when our time comes, will the fruit of our lives have ripened enough to nourish others, and will the seeds of what Christ cultivated within us continue to grow long after we are gone?

The fruit isn't merely proof that the tree lived. It is what the tree gives back to life.
